issues.legal_issue: An agricultural-tenancy enactment is protected from an estate-based constitutional challenge when the land falls within the local equivalent of an estate under the existing law on land tenures, even if that law does not use the word “estate.”
material_facts: The petitions challenged the constitutional validity of an enactment extending agricultural-tenancy provisions to the lands concerned.

The applicable land-revenue code did not use the word “estate,” but defined tenure-holders as persons holding land from the State and provided for classes of such tenure-holders, including occupants of the relevant kind.
The landholders held the lands under the State and paid land revenue for them.
The code’s provisions, read with the enactment’s definitions, showed that the lands were held under tenures that were in substance estates.
issues.conclusion: The lands fell within the local equivalents of an estate, so the enactment was protected from the constitutional challenge on that ground. The petitions were dismissed with costs.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(2)(a) includes both an estate and its local equivalent as understood under the existing law relating to land tenures in the relevant area. The relevant definitions in sections 2(17) and 2(18) of the challenged enactment and sections 2(20), 27, 145 and 146 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, read together, showed that land held by a tenure-holder from the State was in substance an estate. The Court relied on Sri Ram Narain Medhi v. The State of Bombay, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 489, which had upheld analogous legislation where the relevant lands came within the meaning of estate under the applicable land-revenue law.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge_to_agricul: A person brings a constitutional writ challenge to a law regulating agricultural tenancies.
predicates.land_held_under_state: The landholder holds the land under the State.
predicates.land_revenue_paid: The landholder pays land revenue for the land.
predicates.tenure_law_recognizes_state_held_land_as: The existing law on land tenures treats the landholder’s State-held land as a tenure, even if it does not use the word “estate.”

issues.definition: When an agricultural-tenancy law is challenged by constitutional writ and the land is held under the State, land revenue is paid, and the tenure law recognizes that State-held land as a tenure, the law is protected from an estate-based constitutional challenge.
